test.name: Short Latin burial entry: translate and explain the key term concisely
test.description: The user pastes a single short Latin burial entry and asks what it says, flagging one word ('relicta') they don't know. Tests that the skill translates the short entry and — the point of the test — explains the genealogically significant term rather than giving a bare literal gloss. Probes the Genealogical context dimension plus proportionate scoping: a one-line entry warrants a concise translation and a focused term explanation, not a heavyweight multi-phase workflow. Reframed from an earlier no-record 'what does [term] mean?' phrasing: a bare single-word question no longer routes to the skill (the model answers it inline, so activation was a hard 0), whereas embedding the record restores reliable activation while keeping the same Genealogical-context probe.

input.user_message: Can you read this Latin burial entry and tell me what it says? I'm especially stuck on the word 'relicta': 'Die 3 Aprilis 1748 sepulta est Maria, relicta Joannis Hofer.'

judge_context: Should translate the short entry faithfully: on 3 April 1748, Maria was buried, the `relicta` (widow) of Joannis Hofer.
Should explain that `relicta` means 'widow' — literally 'the one left behind' / 'relict' — i.e. a woman whose husband has already died; here Maria is the widow of Joannis Hofer.

Should explain the genealogical significance: it tells the researcher the husband (Joannis Hofer) predeceased this 1748 burial, so they can look for his death or burial before this date, and it confirms a prior marriage. May note the husband's name is in the genitive case (`Joannis` = of Johannes), so his nominative name is Joannes/Johannes.

Answer should be proportionate to a one-line entry — a concise translation and a focused explanation of the term, not a heavyweight multi-phase transcription/extraction workflow (offering record-extraction as an optional next step is fine).
May helpfully note the masculine form `relictus` (widower) so the researcher recognizes the term for either spouse.
